why: It states that Japan protected hooves with straw until Meiji, which is why these maps give a courier station a sandal supply rather than a shoeing forge. It does not say nails were unknown before Meiji. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources.

It states the door rule of a Beijing range plainly, a three-bay range with a door only in its middle bay, which is the Beijing (north Chinese) courtyard house's form of one door for several bays. The article itself sets the Beijing house apart from courtyard houses in Shanxi, Shaanxi, Sichuan and the south, and does not say whether those regions kept the same door rule. It is unsigned and without sources, and gives no date for the practice it describes; it speaks of the family's north range, not the servants' south range, and says nothing of how servants' rooms were entered.

It describes the canonical Japanese dispersed settlement, the pattern one of our settlement forms is drawn from, and it is the one page read that says where a dispersed farm's household water came from. Its limits are that it dates the channel mesh the household water ran in to the Kaga domain's early-modern works (近世), the era the setting draws on, but gives the household use itself only as "in former times" (かつては), which may reach into the twentieth century; that it speaks of one plain, whose deep water table under a fan is not every dispersed plain's; and that "in many areas" leaves the rest unsaid. The practice presupposes a channel mesh that passes every farm; a dispersed plain without one is not described here.

It gives the charcoal consumed against the steel produced, which is the fuel hunger this page argues from. It ties the product to swords and says nothing of hooves. The tonnages are given with no date and no attribution to a period smelt; they describe the standardized run of the kind carried out today for swordsmiths, not an Edo ledger.

It says what the hundred articles are: a longer text on how the shogunate was to be run, at least partly drafted by Ieyasu's successors. Its sentence on authorship has no footnote of its own, and it is a weak witness on authorship, since it presents the short maxim as Ieyasu's words of 1604 where Japanese Wikipedia holds it a later composition, first credited to him in print in 1835. Gubbins's 1919 paper, one of the translations it cites and readable as a scan, dates the compilation to the third shogun's reign from evidence in the text itself (the junior council, set up in 1633; Nagasaki as the only port, from 1641) and is the closer source.

It states what the iron was made into and how the refining hearth worked - pig iron reheated and its carbon burned down under the bellows - which is what this page's account of a smelting valley's works rests on.

It defines the system - canals joined to reservoirs and ponds, drawing, storing and lifting water together - and names the Baiqi canal of the Warring States period as the earliest, which puts the form before modern times. It says the modern form was developed in the late 1950s from older pond and canal works and suits hill country. It is an unsigned reference entry on China Agriculture Press's knowledge platform that cites no period text, and it gives no count or size of the ponds on an early system.

It states that the sandals were cheap, quickly worn out and easily replaced, which is why a courier station on these maps stocks them. Its limits are that it is a trade blog retelling a traveler's account rather than scholarship, and that it gives no rate of wear per distance. The observations are of Meiji Japan in the 1890s.

It gives the bay count of the six offices at the top of the provincial hierarchy, the higher half of the record's one comparison of the six offices across ranks; the county's two bays come from other sources, not from this essay. It is a magazine essay; its counts are of the buildings standing today, restored (the essay says only that the eastern side was opened after restoration), at one yamen of exceptional rank, and its comparison with county yamen - that the layout is much the same, and the yamen less imposing than the writer expected - is an impression. A count of bays is not a size: the essay gives neither a bay's width nor its depth, which a higher seat's halls may have had larger, so three bays against two compares bays, not floor area, and cannot by itself set a ceiling on how much larger a higher seat's office was.

It gives the Tateyama office's area in tsubo and its size against the West office, which sets a shogunal magistracy outside Edo beside Edo's own. It does not attribute its area figure in the text or say what year it describes; among its references is the Nagasaki Prefecture Board of Education's excavation report on the site (長崎県文化財調査報告書146, 1998), the likely origin and the source to read for the number. The figure is the whole compound - the magistrate's residence, longhouses, storehouses and a riding ground as well as the offices - and one of the magistracy's two offices, the West office standing as well at about half its area; its "about 10,000 square meters" rounds down, since 3,278.5 tsubo is about 10,800. The Nagasaki magistrate's office also handled foreign trade and diplomacy, so its size reflects duties no domain office had.

It states that the communities stood on riverbanks because tanning needed the water and that they were registered and settled apart, as separate villages or as parts of towns, which is the siting this page's tanning yard and outcaste quarter follow. It gives no siege rationale and no distance.

It states where the communities stood - the village edge, beside a river - and what work the status carried: disposing of fallen cattle and horses, hide work, leather goods, sandals, lamp wicks, and the executioner's, constable's and watchman's duties. It is a national generalization and names no particular castle town. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources.

It states the brewer's standing as local elite with a shop at the center of town, which is why this page keeps the brewery in town rather than at its edge. It gives no count of brewers per town and no building sizes. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. The article runs down to the modern trade, so the shop at the center is read as the early-modern form.

It states that the collar was worn continuously for up to several months and shows the magistrate's seal on the boards, which is the public half of the punishment this page draws. It gives no statutory table of terms. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. The seal cited is read off a photograph of about 1870, a late-Qing object rather than a statute.

It states the siting and gives the shogunate's motive as deterrence, which is what this page's rule about the ground standing on the busiest way rests on. Its limits are that it is signed only with the site's name, with no citations a reader can follow (it names the 公事方御定書 of 1742 in its text), and that the motive is its reading of the record rather than a quoted ordinance.

It states that a village punished breaches of its own code by banishment, which is the ceiling this page gives village authority. It does not say that nothing heavier was ever available to a village. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources.

It gives the tower's height and its three stories, the one Japanese time-bell tower this page sizes against. It gives no base dimension and the town's population is not on it. The 16 m is the height of the 1894 rebuilding after the town fire, the fourth tower on the site, not a measured Edo tower.

It gives the tower's 21 m square platform pierced by a cross vault and the city's character as a Ming garrison, which is the street-arch tower type this page keeps off a small county seat. The dimensions carry no citation on the page, whose one reference is the heritage listing, and they describe the platform after its repair of 1777.

It states that the circle was a tenement institution around a shared well, which is why this page counts the dense well pattern as urban rather than village density. It gives no households-per-well figure. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. It dates the practice only as former.

It states that the tenements drew from shared aqueduct wells and that the samurai districts were supplied first with the remainder going to the townspeople, which is the shared-draw pattern and the status distinction this page's wells follow. It describes the shogunal capital, the largest system in the country.

It states the inspection-and-toll function and where the stations stood, which is the institution behind the tariff posts these maps place at the gates by the setting's canon. The historical stations stood on the roads rather than on a city's gates, a difference this page states.
It states that a post station kept horses and porters permanently for the official relay beside its inns, which is the wayside facility with stabling this page names. It says nothing of pasture.

It gives the wood consumed per unit of charcoal - about four and a half to one by weight in a working pit - which is the ratio that sends the kiln to the wood on these maps. The method it documents is the earth pit itself, close to a premodern burn; the ratio is a yield of one method at one size, so it bounds rather than measures a household's burn.

It states that the lower residences were large garden estates in the outskirts used as villas and fire refuges while the working residence stood nearest the castle, which is the pattern of roomier estates outside this page draws. It describes daimyo under alternate attendance in Edo, an institution a domain seat's own samurai did not have. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources.

It gives a horse's daily water and the multiplier under hard work, which sizes the watering a courier or wagon yard must supply. The figure is keyed to a modern horse of 450 kg; the horses of a premodern East Asian post road were far smaller, so the intake carried onto these maps is an upper figure.
It states the buffalo's need to wallow to keep cool, which is why a livery yard on these maps offers a buffalo more than a trough. Its daily water intake is not on it.
It states that whole trains were lodged and watered from a courtyard well or fountain, the relay-watering pattern this page's livery yard follows. It makes no comparison with multiplying basins.

It gives the throughput of one busy street trough in a day, which is the turnover figure this page's relay watering rests on. Its limits are that it is a guidebook's 1879 claim, and that Victorian London's horse traffic is a far larger case than a provincial livery yard. And a Victorian street trough was fed continuously from the water mains, while a yard basin on these maps is filled by bucket from a well, so the throughput does not carry across as a bound on how many animals one basin serves.

It gives the tower's height and its singularity in the town, which is the county-tier anchor this page's tower glyph is sized to. Pingyao was an unusually rich merchant town, so its tower is a generous county anchor; the height is the same figure the Chinese Wikipedia entry carries, so the two do not corroborate one another; and the English page is a machine rendering of the Chinese.

It states the paired form as the usual arrangement, the combined single tower as a variant, and the towers' duty of announcing the time, which is the county-seat tower these maps draw. It gives no rule about how many towers a county seat had. The article is a stub carrying the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks references.
It defines the form as the official compound's own timekeeping building, the variant this page names beside the freestanding tower. The page carries no references at all and fixes no period.
It places a county town's drum tower at the exact center of its crossroads, which is the siting these maps give the tower.

It states that the qiaolou was part of the prefectural office compound, which is why this page calls it the compound's own tower rather than a poor seat's substitute. It does not say the tower stood over the compound's gate. The building is of the tenth to thirteenth centuries, several centuries before the Ming and Edo anchors these maps take.

It states that the bell was run at public expense on a fee levied from the roughly four hundred blocks that could hear it, and lists the city's other time bells, all but this one at temples, which is the earshot anchor and the temple-bell pattern this page uses. The fee is per ken of frontage, not per household.

It states that the watches were relayed through the streets by walking watchmen, which is how one tower's signal reached a whole city and why this page gives a capital no second tower. Much of the article documents modern survivals and regions outside the setting's Chinese core, so the imperial-era dating of the relayed watch rests on its general framing.

It gives the capital's one pair of towers timing the watches for the whole inner city, the China-first scaling answer this page sets against Edo's many bells. It describes the imperial capital, a ceiling rather than a norm.

It gives the direction and Edo's guardian temple in it, which is the bearing this page reads the city's northern institutions against. The alignment of execution ground, pleasure quarter and outcaste head's compound to it is this page's reading.

It records where the quarter was moved to, which is one of the three places this page aligns to Edo's northeast. It says nothing of the kimon or of direction. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. And the article gives its own reason for the move - the city had grown and daimyo residences had come up against the quarter, and it infers that the competition from bathhouses was a further reason - which competes with the northeast reading this page draws from the places. It also names the two sites the shogunate weighed, Nihon-zutsumi or Honjo, and Honjo lies east across the Sumida rather than northeast, so by the article's account direction did not fix the choice. For the quarter's own form it gives the first site's size, and, in the uncited caption of a late-Edo plan of the second site, the high wall, the ditch (ohaguro-dobu) and the single approach by Emon-zaka and the Gojikken road - the new quarter's form at the end of the period, not evidence for the first site, and a caption that warns the plan's proportions are distorted (the real quarter was longer top to bottom and narrower side to side than drawn); and it gives the second site's size twice in figures that do not agree (3 cho square and a little over 20,000 tsubo); it describes one quarter, the most isolated of the three great ones, not the usual form.

It states the name, the trades and the riverbed siting with both reasons, which is the riverside outcaste quarter this page draws. The name is one they were called, not one they gave themselves. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. Its subject is medieval Kyoto, earlier than most of what these maps draw from.

It describes an outcaste head's precinct standing inside the city as an enclosed block with residences, storehouses, a shrine, a court and a jail, which is the in-city outcaste quarter this page argues for. It does not say where the residents worked. And the compound was the headquarters of the man who administered every eta community in eastern Japan, inside the largest city in the country, with a court and a jail because it held delegated jurisdiction; an ordinary provincial seat's outcaste block is a far smaller and plainer thing.

It states that the boards stood where traffic was frequent - at post stations and barriers - which is the traffic siting this page's board follows. The article is a few paragraphs on two references, one of them another wiki, and it says what the Japanese article cited beside it says, so the two are not independent.

It states that the headman copied and relayed the lord's circulars and needed reading, writing and the abacus for the office, which is the one reader per settlement this page's notice board depends on. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources.

It states that a kawara roof is repaired tile by tile, which is why this page counts a tiled roof as a lasting one. It gives no lifespan. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks citations and may hold original research.

It states that line villages follow natural levees and the spring line at the foot of the hills, the easy-water ground this page's dispersed households sit on. The passage dates nothing and its examples are present-day villages, so it establishes the landform logic rather than that premodern villages were sited so.

It states that the district boundaries within a province - not domain borders - were to be drawn clearly and variances settled by inquiry before the map was made up, which is the authenticity this page claims for a drawn line.

It gives the crushing and sorting of the kera and the finishing of part of it into wrought iron, the sequence this page's smelting valley follows. The crushing and sorting is dated to the 1750s, while the finishing of fractions at the smithy into wrought iron sits in the article's account of the modern Yasukuni tatara, so the sequence's seventeenth-century date rests on the paper cited beside it.

It shows one other tradition soaking hides in standing vats rather than a current, the pit-soaking form a ditch-fed yard on these maps falls back to. It is one Moroccan case; it does not speak for every other tradition.
It gives the scale of a medieval kiln district in kiln sites, which is the real size this page's one drawn works stands down from. It does not give distribution or workers' residence.
It records fire ordinances restricting fire-using trades inside the dense town, the fire law this page's kiln siting rests on. No passage names kilns.

It defines the status and lists its occupations, none of them a craft, which is what this page's separation of the potter from the outcaste rests on. That potters were not of the status is drawn from the list's silence, not stated on the page.

It states that ware kilns were built beside tile kilns at the same sites, which is why these maps draw one works for both. It is ancient, not Edo, and speaks of kilns side by side rather than one kiln firing both.
It states that fired clay survives where organic goods rot, which is why this page treats every settlement's ceramics as a steady demand a works must meet.
It gives the rule by which heavy, cheap goods are made near their market, which this page applies to storage jars. The application to ceramics is this page's own.
It states that farriers traditionally worked from a forge with a yard for hot-shoeing, which is the premises this page's smith apron draws. It carries no size.
It states that smiths worked in small shops, often at the center of a village or town, which is the modest premises this page gives a town smith. It carries no measurement.

It gives the Tang network's 1,639 stations and the Han's spacing of a station every thirty li, the comparison figure for the setting's own denser courier network. The setting's road mileage and courier counts are the GM's canon. The count and the spacing come from different dynasties, the count cited to the 大唐六典 and the spacing given for the Han.

It states that iron shoes became common in China only from the Yuan and that earlier hoof protection was wrapped or strapped, which is why this page does not rest its argument on Chinese practice. It does not say whether the Yuan shoes were nailed.
It states that the Roman device was strapped on rather than nailed, one of the two comparisons this page considered and set aside. It does not mention the imperial post.
It states that the hulling and polishing was the shop's own work, which is why the rice dealer draws as an ordinary shop with no separate mill.

It describes the treadle pestle this page puts in a rice dealer's shop. It does not say where the tool stood. The article is a stub carrying the encyclopedia's own notice that it needs sources, and it dates and locates the tool nowhere.

It places the northern execution ground about two ri, five miles, out along the highway, which is the distance behind this page's rule that a ground hugs a road rather than a gate. The two ri is the page's distance to the post town; that the ground in the town just south of it stood about as far out is this page's reading of two sentences.

It states that the main gate of an early-modern castle stood at the front, usually the south, with the rear gate opposite, which is the pair and the aspect our capital's castle draws. It gives no reason for the aspect and nothing on divination.
It defines the sarae this page names as a moat's maintenance and attests the practice in the Edo period, for rivers. It says nothing of moats.

It gives the measured size of a surviving domain-seat samurai residence and the stipend band of its households, the anchor this page checks its detached samurai house against. Its "about 67 tsubo" is the main house alone, without the long gatehouse, and it is the house as restored in 2016-2018 to Meiji-period drawings after several enlargements and alterations since the 1733 rebuilding: it gives the house as it stood by the Meiji era, not surely as its Edo households had it. Its households were retainers of 500 to 1,000 koku, an upper case beside the poor samurai of our terrace houses.
It dates the ranking of City God temples down to the county, which is why a county seat on these maps carries one beside its yamen.

It states the tenure arrangement thought to be a major cause of the dispersed pattern, the reason this page gives for its dispersed hamlets. The arrangement is a cultivation right rather than a land grant, and the reclamation runs from the late Sengoku into mid-Edo.
It states what the rick is and when it stood, the seasonal feature these maps leave undrawn. It gives no standing duration and does not use the Toyama word waraguro.
It states where a clustered village arose - the foot of a hill, a river terrace, a crossroads - and describes the houses gathered in an irregular lump, the knoll cluster these maps draw.

It states the row form and its reason - the farmland beside the dwelling saves transport - which is the linear settlement category this page places its strung-out hamlets in. A German form used as the documented type; the setting's villages are not German.
It lists the eight buildings of a headman's compound, the top of the farmstead ladder these maps draw the typical plot below. A reconstruction; it describes one class of farmhouse in one province.

It states that a complex farmhouse plan is the standard type with rooms added, the growth by addition these maps' varied houses follow; its Nipponica entry reports the eighteenth-century count of house sizes in villages near Utsunomiya, from floor plans drawn up to lodge the shogun's retainers; and the Heibonsha World Encyclopedia entry on the same page classifies roof shapes, roofing materials and the regional plan forms. It gives no proportions and no direction of growth, the house count gives floor areas for one district and no length or depth, and the regional forms come with no share of households.
It defines the shed a farm kept its crop and tools in, the commoner outbuilding these maps draw beside the rarer storehouse.
It states the doma's uses - meals after work, drying the crop, weaving sandals, tending tools - the working floor this page gives a household without a shed. It does not call the doma a store.
It describes the labor the walls took and what a farmhouse stored, the construction behind this page's reading of the kura as a wealth marker. It does not price the building.
It states the seat principle a dwelling was sited by, the hill behind and water before that this page's clusters answer to. Its water is a watercourse or pond, not paddy.
It defines the dispersed form and gives both its names and readings, the form and the words this page uses for its dispersed hamlets. It does not say how a steading was reached.

It states that the back lane and the main street together framed the planned village and that the lane divided the village from its fields, which is the field-ward edge this page draws. The English planned village, stated as such.

It states that a back lane at the far end of the plots gives a planned village its regular layout, the device this page's back lane reproduces. The English medieval case, which the page cites as such.

It states that the lanes were the public space all the houses faced and used, the socially live lane this page draws in a village. A modern urban form standing in for a village's; the scale and the century both differ.

It gives the modern sanitary rule that a well stands uphill and some twenty meters from an animal yard, the contamination this page's byre-and-well spacing answers. A modern engineering manual for the tropics.

It states that a community's watering place served its beasts and its humans alike, which is why a village well on these maps may have a trough beside it. A largely Western institution; it names springs, not wells, as where troughs stood.

It states the privy-and-pigsty grouping and its antiquity, the manure economy behind this page's siting of the animal facilities with the latrine. It speaks of pigsties, not of cattle sheds or chicken houses.
It defines where a household's bulk vegetables and dry crops were grown, which is why the dooryard bed on these maps is small. It draws no line between a field and a kitchen garden.

It states that rice is cut in autumn and dried on racks in the field before threshing, which is why a paddy household's yard needs less threshing floor than a dry-grain one and why its season is the autumn. It gives no drying time and names no month for threshing.
